title: Who ran it
lede: Roles are as described in the sources cited. Later careers are included only where we found a source.

people.name: Isao Okawa
people.text: Founder of the CSK Group and Sega’s main backer. In January 2001 he gave the company his Sega shares and other assets, producing a ¥77.9 billion gain.[^2]

people.name: Shoichiro Irimajiri
people.text: Set two hardware teams against each other in 1997: Hideki Sato’s in Japan and an outside group in the United States.[^7]

people.name: Hideki Sato
people.text: Designed the Saturn and led the winning Dreamcast design. He announced the end of production at the Tokyo news conference on January 31, 2001.[^7][^4]

people.name: Bernie Stolar
people.text: Rebuilt the U.S. company and its retail relationships, bought Visual Concepts and refused EA’s terms. Replaced five weeks before launch.[^7][^16]

people.name: Peter Moore
people.role: Marketing chief, then president, Sega of America
people.text: Joined from Reebok in early 1999, ran the 9/9/99 launch and became president in May 2000.[^6][^21] He delivered the exit announcement in the United States.[^9]
people.later: Joined Microsoft in 2003 and Electronic Arts in 2007.[^8][^9]

people.name: Charles Bellfield
people.role: VP communications, later strategy, Sega of America
people.text: Co-wrote the September 2000 paper advising Tokyo to leave hardware. His verdict: “Money. Money talks. You need a budget.”[^7]

people.name: Toshiro Kezuka
people.role: Vice-chairman and COO, Sega of America, from Aug 1999
people.text: Named to the top U.S. post on August 4, 1999 in place of Stolar.[^16]

people.name: Bing Gordon
people.text: The EA executive quoted as saying the Dreamcast could not succeed without EA. He later said Sega “was not acting like a competent hardware company.”[^7]
